title: What regulatory sandboxes did — and didn’t — deliver
label: Regulatory sandboxes · CFIT view
summary: The committee questioned Anna Wallace, who set up the FCA’s 2016 regulatory sandbox and now leads CFIT, about what sandboxes actually do, what they have achieved, where they fall short, and how industry-led coalitions might fill the gaps. Wallace explained how sandboxes work in practice, gave examples (including a cross‑firm Digital Company ID project moving into the FCA sandbox), and argued for a wider ecosystem approach — more industry collaboration, shared standards for AI, better evidence of long-term consumer impact, and care over intellectual property and anti‑competitive risks.

speakers.label: Anna Wallace
speakers.name: Anna Wallace
speakers.role: Chief Executive Officer, Centre for Finance, Innovation and Technology (CFIT)

glossary.definition: A controlled environment where firms test financial products with real customers under temporary regulatory relief so regulators can learn and give tailored feedback.
A limited, time‑bound licence allowing a firm to operate while proving its product or business model.
A regulator's informal assurance not to take enforcement action while a firm runs a specific test, similar to a safe harbour.
Regulator advice tailored to one firm about how existing rules apply to its specific test or product.
Centre for Finance, Innovation and Technology — a body that brings industry, regulators and government together to prototype market solutions.
A temporary removal or relaxation of a regulatory requirement for a firm or test.
Automated, algorithm-driven financial advice often delivered online with limited human intervention.

chapters.title: What a sandbox actually is
chapters.takeaway: A sandbox gives short-term regulatory space to test products with consumers, using tools like restricted permissions, tailored guidance, or no‑action letters, and regulators build consumer protections into trials.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Anna, could you start by explaining your background and the basic idea of the sandbox?

turns.speaker: Anna Wallace
turns.text: I set up the FCA’s original sandbox in 2016 and ran it until 2020. I now run CFIT, which builds industry coalitions to prototype solutions and feed successful pilots into regulatory sandboxes.

turns.speaker: Lord Lilley
turns.text: People asked me to explain a sandbox. Walk me through a simple example: what steps happen when a firm comes in?

turns.speaker: Anna Wallace
turns.text: Three practical tools were used. One was restricted permission — a time‑limited licence to test with real customers. Second was individual guidance telling a firm how rules applied in its case. Third was a no‑enforcement‑action letter, a limited safe harbour. Each test had lots of regulator due diligence and built‑in consumer protections, like limits on who could join and compensation pots.

turns.speaker: Lord Lilley
turns.text: What if the product turns out to be harmful?

turns.speaker: Anna Wallace
turns.text: We assessed likely harms before approval, limited participation to suitable customers, required compensation arrangements, and could stop the test. If firms couldn’t meet those protective measures, they couldn’t test.

chapters.title: Did sandboxes deliver market-changing innovation?
chapters.takeaway: Sandboxes helped some firms get to market faster and attract funding, but evidence of broad consumer or market transformation is limited and needs longer-term study.

turns.speaker: Lord Eatwell
turns.text: Sandboxes have been around a while but I can’t point to blockbuster innovations that came specifically from them. Why hasn’t the idea had bigger market impact?

turns.speaker: Anna Wallace
turns.text: We saw firm‑level benefits: faster market entry, easier funding access. The Bank for International Settlements compared cohorts and found those benefits on the firm side. But attributing wide consumer or structural market changes needs a longitudinal study — we don't yet have clear long‑run evidence.

turns.speaker: Lord Eatwell
turns.text: Some innovations are wholesale, not consumer facing — like credit default swaps — so how do you judge 'consumer benefit'?

turns.speaker: Anna Wallace
turns.text: You have to look through wholesale effects to end users. The sandbox helped explore infrastructure ideas — for example, distributed ledger work — but connecting those trials to consumer outcomes was and remains hard to prove.

turns.speaker: Baroness Donaghy
turns.text: Costs are raised again and again. Is the cost of entry a barrier, and does the FCA favour applicants?

turns.speaker: Anna Wallace
turns.text: Costs to firms and the FCA were monitored. Early evaluation showed the sandbox reduced time and cost to market for many firms versus the usual authorisation routes. The FCA tried to avoid unfair advantage by publishing participants and the tests, but keeping the balance between helping small innovators and avoiding preferential treatment is an ongoing concern.

turns.speaker: Lord Sharkey
turns.text: Why haven't we seen a fresh, quantified cost‑benefit analysis since 2017, and how are lessons shared outside the sandbox?

turns.speaker: Anna Wallace
turns.text: The 2017 'Lessons Learned' report addressed many of those evaluation points for the original design. The FCA has produced other updates, and participants were published. When a trial points to policy change, that triggers formal policy work (and more standard CBA). But because sandboxes are operational, not law‑making, they don't always sit in the same CBA framework.

turns.speaker: Lord Sharkey
turns.text: Do sandbox learnings ever remain proprietary to participants?

turns.speaker: Anna Wallace
turns.text: Participants got regulatory feedback specific to them, which could be commercially useful. The FCA kept rights to share regulatory insights; firms had to agree in advance about what would be published so useful learning could be transmitted without forcing disclosure of core trade secrets.

chapters.title: Where CFIT fits and who benefits
chapters.takeaway: CFIT brings firms, regulators and government together to solve shared market problems before or alongside sandboxes — for example, a multi‑firm Digital Company ID moving into the FCA sandbox — and it pushes for public‑value outcomes and wider adoption.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How does CFIT interact with the FCA sandbox?

turns.speaker: Anna Wallace
turns.text: CFIT runs open coalitions to tackle market failures: industry, regulators and government identify barriers, prototype minimum viable products, and create evidence for scale-up. One coalition, Digital Company ID, formed a multi‑firm consortium that the FCA agreed to take into its sandbox.

turns.speaker: Lord Davies of Brixton
turns.text: Is a sandbox mainly facilitation rather than invention — does it encourage or actually create new ideas?

turns.speaker: Anna Wallace
turns.text: Mainly it facilitates. It helps firms test regulated deployment and lowers regulatory risk, which encourages investors and incumbents to act, but it doesn’t invent ideas out of nowhere.

turns.speaker: Lord Turnbull
turns.text: Do we have clear success stories — companies that graduated and became mainstream successes?

turns.speaker: Anna Wallace
turns.text: There are firms from early cohorts that grew significantly; one early participant is now valued at over £100m. But success is multi‑dimensional: product survival, wider market adoption, partnerships with incumbents, or influencing infrastructure. We need systematic follow‑up to map progression reliably.

turns.speaker: Lord Turnbull
turns.text: When the FCA helps a firm discover something useful, does it have a duty to spread that around?

turns.speaker: Anna Wallace
turns.text: Yes — the FCA typically publishes cohorts and thematic insights and issues guidance when warranted. Deciding when to publish and how much to protect firm IP is a judgement made case by case.

turns.speaker: Lord Sharkey
turns.text: Who owns sandbox data and IP?

turns.speaker: Anna Wallace
turns.text: It’s complex. Participants keep proprietary IP; the FCA retained rights to share regulatory findings and required firms to agree in advance what could be published so lessons could be spread without breaking confidentiality.

chapters.title: Cross-cutting issues: AI, international lessons and next steps
chapters.takeaway: Sandboxes matter for regulator learning and AI testing, but industry, government and standard‑setting must act too; the UK should couple sandboxes with cross‑industry coordination, shared standards and better long‑term evidence.

turns.speaker: Lord Hollick
turns.text: How should sandboxes handle AI, including agentic AI and payments agents?

turns.speaker: Anna Wallace
turns.text: AI raises standards, assurance, data, identity, consent and liability questions. The FCA’s AI sandbox can help regulators learn, but industry needs shared assurance methods and infrastructure. CFIT wants to help build those standards so smaller firms and SMEs aren’t left behind.

turns.speaker: Lord Hollick
turns.text: What about influencers pushing financial products — do sandboxes help with that risk?

turns.speaker: Anna Wallace
turns.text: CFIT hasn't focused on influencers. From my FCA experience, the rules aim to catch financial promotions done 'by means of business' regardless of platform. It's enforcement‑heavy and technology‑intensive; AI tools are now used to monitor it.

turns.speaker: Lord Vaux of Harrowden
turns.text: Other countries copied sandboxes. Are there lessons from abroad?

turns.speaker: Anna Wallace
turns.text: The UK linked the sandbox to market failures and had strong resourcing early, which helped. Cross‑sector or cross‑border sandboxes were tried elsewhere but often came too soon. Some countries allow long or indefinite waivers; that should trigger policy or regulatory change if a waiver becomes permanent.

turns.speaker: Lord Eatwell
turns.text: Overall, has the sandbox worked?

turns.speaker: Anna Wallace
turns.text: It worked in parts: accelerating firms, helping regulators learn, and informing policy (crypto and advice were examples). But we need more evidence on long‑run consumer impact. Also, some gaps — market infrastructure, trust, and cross‑industry standards — aren’t solved by a sandbox alone.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If you could improve one thing about sandboxes now, what would it be?

turns.speaker: Anna Wallace
turns.text: Do more ecosystem work before and alongside sandboxes: industry coalitions, shared standards, and clear routes to scale. And commission a longitudinal study to measure consumer and market impact over 10 years.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you — that gives us a practical view of what sandboxes did, where they helped, and what’s still missing.
